name: The Pareto Principle
aliases: The law of the vital few
statement: Roughly 80 percent of results come from 20 percent of causes.
meaning: The Pareto principle holds that for many outcomes, about eighty per cent of the consequences come from around twenty per cent of the causes — a small fraction of inputs accounting for most of the output. It is the idea of the vital few and the trivial many: that effort, sales, faults, or wealth are typically concentrated in a minority of their sources rather than spread evenly.
mechanism: The eighty-twenty split is a special case of a power-law distribution, the Pareto distribution, in which a few large contributors dominate a long tail of small ones. The specific split corresponds to a particular value of the distribution's shape parameter, so it is not privileged: distributions with different exponents give ninety-ten, ninety-nine-one, or other splits. The principle captures the concentration such heavy-tailed distributions produce, but the exact numbers are illustrative, not fixed.

examples.text: Pareto's original observation was that about eighty per cent of Italy's land was owned by roughly twenty per cent of the population, a concentration he found recurring elsewhere.

The adages that most sales come from a minority of customers, and that a small share of code accounts for most bugs — Microsoft reported that fixing the top fifth of reported bugs removed some eighty per cent of related crashes.
Quality control uses a bar chart of defect causes ordered by frequency to find the vital few problems worth fixing first — a tool Juran brought into the field.

variants.name: The Pareto distribution
variants.text: The underlying power law, whose shape parameter sets how concentrated the outcomes are; different exponents yield splits other than eighty-twenty.

variants.name: The vital few and the useful many
variants.text: Juran's later revision of his own phrase, replacing trivial with useful to stop the remaining majority being dismissed as worthless.

whyItMatters: It is one of the most widely used rules of thumb in management, quality control, and time management, a quick guide to where effort will pay off most: focus on the minority of causes that drive the majority of effects. Rooted in the real mathematics of heavy-tailed distributions, it captures a genuine and recurring feature of how outcomes concentrate, even as the precise figures vary.

working.text: identify the small share of causes, customers, or faults that drives most of the effect, and concentrate effort there.
use a Pareto chart or ranking to attack the largest contributors first rather than treating all causes equally.
take eighty-twenty as illustrative, expecting the real ratio to vary by domain rather than holding exactly.

limits: The eighty-twenty numbers are a rough heuristic, not a law; the actual split varies widely by domain, and it need not be eighty-twenty at all. The two figures need not even sum to a hundred, since they measure different things — the share of causes and the share of effects — so ninety-ten or seventy-twenty are equally possible. It is descriptive, not predictive: it summarises observed concentration but guarantees no particular split in a new setting, and it describes many but not all distributions, only the heavy-tailed ones. The percentages are often quoted without evidence.
misreadings: It is not always exactly eighty-twenty; that is an approximation, and real ratios range across seventy-thirty, ninety-ten, ninety-nine-one, and more. The two numbers do not have to add to a hundred, because they count different quantities. And it is not a proven law of nature but an empirical rule of thumb, apt to be misapplied when the numbers are cited as if fixed.
origin: Rooted in Vilfredo Pareto's 1896 observation of the concentration of Italian land ownership; generalised and named the Pareto principle by the quality-management pioneer Joseph Juran, who coined the vital few and the trivial many, from around 1941.
